articles.title: The pet I’ll never forget: the tiny horse with a big personality – who helps psychiatric patients
articles.summary: Black Pearl is a therapy animal, who works with military veterans. This sweet show-off has completely changed my life. I trained and competed in dressage for many years and after I retired, I decided to buy a miniature horse for company at home in southern California.
body: I started training her for fun and began to teach her tricks. She learned quickly. I thought of a great way to give back to the community – Black Pearl and I could find ways to help people. I started to wonder where I could visit with my little horse.

Black Pearl inspired me to start my charity, Mini Therapy Horses. If it wasn’t for her outgoing personality, I wouldn’t have attempted it. Now I run a programme with her and eight other miniature therapy horses, visiting patients in the lockdown psychiatric unit at a veterans’ hospital in Los Angeles. The vets have been through so much: they have PTSD, traumatic brain injuries and/or drug addiction and many are homeless. They can pet and hug the horses – they love them. It helps them to feel less lonely and isolated.

We also visit several other hospitals – many of the kids and adults are away from home for a long time and the time they spend with our minis is very comforting. If a child is visually impaired we can take their hands and help them to feel our little horses. They can brush their coats and this tactile experience makes them very happy.
points: Black Pearl is a therapy animal, who works with military veterans.

articles.title: Is it true that … drinking alcohol warms you up?
articles.summary: A hot toddy might make you feel toasty, but drinking in cold conditions can be risky. Hot toddies, red wine, a dram of whisky: alcohol has long been a go-to remedy for keeping warm. But while a drink might make you feel warmer, does it actually help?
body: Alcohol affects the body’s temperature-regulating system. Our core body temperature is controlled by the hypothalamus, a region of the brain that helps regulate how we respond to changes in temperature. When we get too hot, blood vessels near the surface of the skin widen, a process known as vasodilation. This allows more warm blood to flow close to the skin, where heat can escape into the surrounding air. When we get too cold, the opposite happens. The blood vessels narrow, or constrict, reducing blood flow to the skin and helping to conserve heat.

Alcohol interferes with this process. It causes blood vessels near the skin to widen, even when our core body temperature has not risen. More warm blood reaches the skin’s surface, which can make us feel hot, and even leave us reaching to take off clothing.
“You’re sending more blood to your skin, which gives you the sensation of feeling warmer,” says Morgan. “But actually you’re not. Your body’s just moving around the blood.”
points: A hot toddy might make you feel toasty, but drinking in cold conditions can be risky.

articles.title: ‘Unable to tell morning from afternoon, I felt my sense of time opening up’: a (mostly dark) winter break in magical Swedish Lapland
articles.summary: With just a few short hours of daylight, the usual boundaries marking time fall away in Abisko, one of the most reliable places to see the northern lights. Looking over the edge of the snow-smoothed canyon down to dark rushing water, we thought we saw a moose or a reindeer, but it could have been a…
body: Travelling to the Arctic Circle in winter had always been a dream, but when I realised the sun wouldn’t get above the horizon on my holiday, it made me twitchy. I usually pack my limited annual leave as tightly as I pack my working life. I was already using up three days’ holiday travelling by train from London to Abisko. How would I make the most of my time there with barely any daylight?

My partner and I chose to stop in this small village in Swedish Lapland almost by chance, when we researched the most northerly stops on the train line between Stockholm and Narvik. Abisko looked on the map like a tiny enclave surrounded by lakes and mountains. Reading more about it, we found that it was home to the Abisko blue hole – a unique microclimate where the geography creates frequent clear skies, making it one of the most reliable places on Earth to see the aurora borealis.
points: With just a few short hours of daylight, the usual boundaries marking time fall away in Abisko, one of the most reliable places to see the northern lights.

articles.title: A new start after 60: At 26, I saw my dream Porsche. At 68, I built one from scratch
articles.summary: Bill Drysdale could never afford the sports car he fell in love with as a young man. So when he retired, he went to night school to learn welding, and began assembling it, bit by bit... When he was 26, Bill Drysdale saw a Porsche 904 at Silverstone racetrack and fell in love.
body: Drysdale grew up in Wigtown, Scotland, and cars were in his blood – his grandfather was chauffeur to the local creamery manager, and he first saw a race with his father, when he was 12 – around the time that his mother went into hospital with multiple sclerosis. Drysdale, an only child, grew close to his father. At 14, he taught him to drive. Together they’d huddle in the kitchen to listen to the Le Mans 24 Hour race on the radio.
Drysdale was only 21 when his dad died; his mother ended up staying in hospital for 23 years. “That made me very independent,” he says. Determined? “Pig-headed, some would say.”

After studying maths and physics at the University of Glasgow, he joined a brake manufacturer as a graduate apprentice engineer. “Oh, it was tremendous,” he says. “As young chaps in the company, there was always this interest in cars and racing and competition.” His favoured form was “sprinting – racing against the clock, competing against yourself”. It was while playing mechanic to a friend in the pit at Silverstone that he saw the Porsche 904 and was floored by “the sound, the look, the line”.

articles.title: Confessions of a Pants Girl: How I Finally Came to Love the Skirt
articles.summary: Pernille Teisbaek on how the recent shows inspired her to revisit the skirt’s place in her wardrobe. Here’s how she’s styling it now.
body: I’ve always been a pants girl. Jeans, low-waisted trousers, oversized sweats—I’ve always gravitated towards pieces you can throw on without overthinking and still feel like yourself. Skirts have never really been off the table, but they’ve only ever played a supporting role in my wardrobe.

That might be about to change. Following the latest shows, I’ve found myself flirting with skirts a little harder. Prada’s spring 2027 show, built around the idea of the skirt—63 of them, to be exact—planted the first seeds in my mind. Green shoots then bloomed after seeing Matthieu Blazy’s spring 2027 collection for Chanel. “For me, the skirt is like a T-shirt. I put all my ideas there,” Mrs. Prada famously stated in a 2006 interview.

articles.title: Inside Kering’s First Water Resilience Lab in Italy
articles.summary: Kering has developed a roadmap for water resilience. There’s a long way to go, but the group says it now has the right building blocks for real change.
body: This story is part of ‘The Business Case for Nature’, a series exploring fashion’s impact on nature and vice versa.

In 1966, the banks of the Arno river burst, causing the most destructive flood Florence had ever experienced. It took dozens of lives, displaced thousands of people, and claimed millions of rare books and art works.

The region has seen many more floods since then. In 2023, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni declared a state of emergency for the worst-hit areas amid Storm Ciarán, which caused an estimated €1.89 billion in damages. One of the fashion suppliers hit was Prato-based Beste Group, whose HQ sits directly on the bank of the Bisenzio river. The company purchased a new machine — worth around €7 million — the month prior, which was then destroyed by the floods. It was only insured for 60% of the price, so replacing it cost the company several million euros. On top of that, the waist-high water brought production to a standstill for three weeks.
points: Kering has developed a roadmap for water resilience.
There’s a long way to go, but the group says it now has the right building blocks for real change.

articles.title: As Midterms Approach, US Consumer Anxiety Is High — But Fashion Is Set to Rally
articles.summary: US luxury spending has propped up the industry in 2026. Does heightened anxiety about the economy risk puncturing the boost?
body: Ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections, US consumer anxiety is at a high.

Thirty-four percent of respondents to an Economist /YouGov survey conducted in October considered the economy and inflation to be the most important issues facing the US. Sixty-seven percent of respondents said they disapproved of President Trump’s handling of inflation. And, when asked how they felt about their futures compared to 10 years ago, 48% said they were more pessimistic.

As reports of consumer sentiment edging close to all-time lows in the weeks leading up to the midterm elections (it dipped once again in October, falling to 48 from 48.1 in September, according to the University of Michigan’s consumer survey), luxury conglomerates continued referring to North America as a “bright spot” in their most recent quarterly earnings, reaffirming the United States as the boon that it has been for luxury this past year.

articles.title: Lymphatic Drainage: 4 Simple Habits to Add to Your Daily Routine
articles.summary: From deep breathing to rebounding, experts explain the small daily habits that can help support healthy lymphatic flow—and why it matters beyond depuffing.
body: Lymphatic drainage has become something of a wellness obsession. From sculpting facial massages to body brushes and compression boots, there are seemingly endless ways to coax away puffiness and encourage a more contoured appearance. But the benefits of a healthy lymphatic system extend well beyond what we can see in the mirror.

The lymphatic system is sometimes described as the “Cinderella of medicine”: “underestimated, yet performing a large part of the essential work,” writes cardiothoracic surgeon Dr. Gerald M. Lemole in his book Lymph & Longevity: The Untapped Secret to Health. While its aesthetic benefits have helped bring lymphatic drainage into the mainstream, this intricate network of vessels, nodes, and fluid is fundamental to everything from immune function to maintaining the body's fluid balance.
And, as it turns out, keeping it functioning properly doesn’t necessarily require a standing appointment with your facialist.

Think of the lymphatic system as the body’s behind-the-scenes maintenance crew. Working alongside the circulatory and immune systems, it helps collect excess fluid from tissues, transports immune cells, and carries certain waste products away from cells.
points: From deep breathing to rebounding, experts explain the small daily habits that can help support healthy lymphatic flow—and why it matters beyond depuffing.

articles.title: Salted Coffee Custard Pie
articles.summary: Like a fine cappuccino, but make it pie. The big bonus here is the buttery oatmeal cookie crust—which requires zero pie weights during prebake.
body: If you can’t be fussed with making coffee and dessert after a big holiday dinner, consider this twofer instead. The silky, sliceable, cool custard is rich and intense with two kinds of coffee, while the oatmeal crust is a tweedy-textured study in contrast. It’s prebaked to mitigate sogginess but doesn’t require pie weights. Mascarpone keeps the whipped cream firm and fluffy for a full 24 hours.

Don’t be tempted to skip the cold-brew concentrate. You don’t want regular cold brew, and definitely not brewed and cooled coffee from your coffee machine at home, no matter how fancy. The concentrate (highly recommend Grady’s Cold Brew Coffee Concentrate) is consistent every single time with exactly the right strength to stand up to the dairy and eggs in the filling.
